title: Earl Palmer - Wikipedia
notes: Earl Cyril Palmer, 25 October 1924 - 19 September 2008 (Banning, California). Raised in the Tremé; a tap dancer from five on the black vaudeville circuit with Ida Cox's Darktown Scandals Review; Army in Europe in the war; then piano and percussion at the Grunewald School of Music, where he learned to read. Dave Bartholomew's band from the late 1940s; The Fat Man, I'm Walkin', Tipitina, Tutti Frutti and most of Little Richard's hits, Lawdy Miss Clawdy, I Hear You Knockin'. On The Fat Man: 'That song required a strong afterbeat throughout the whole piece. With Dixieland you had a strong afterbeat only after you got to the shout last chorus.' Reportedly the first to use the word funky to musicians. To Hollywood in 1957 (Aladdin), then the Wrecking Crew; 450 dates in 1967. Film and television scores. Local 47 treasurer 1982-84 and from 1990. Make It Funky! (2005), The Wrecking Crew (2008). Quotations: the New Orleans bass drum's 'parade beat connotation'; to Cracker, 'I invented this shit'. Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, 2000. Singles list: The Fat Man (1949) to Tom Waits (1978), including Slow Down, Dizzy Miss Lizzy and Bony Moronie (Larry Williams, 1958), Rockin' Robin (1958), La Bamba, Donna, Summertime Blues, You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' (1964), River Deep - Mountain High (1966).

title: Tony Scherman, 'What Was Rock and Roll to Me?', from Backbeat: Earl Palmer's Story (Da Capo, 2000), chapter four (excerpt), Among the Musical, 22 May 2025
notes: Palmer in his own words, from the oral biography. Heard Vernel Fournier and Art Blakey the same night after the service: 'that's what got me playing drums'. Bartholomew: 'Earl was better than any drummer they had in New Orleans.' The Louisiana Weekly, 15 March 1947: 'the new sensation on the tubs'. J&M 'hardly bigger than a bedroom'; 'Didn't even have no mike on the drums, just a mike on the bass and piano, one on the vocal, and the one that Tyler and Lee used was pointed at the drums.' 'What was rock and roll to me? I lived in a jazz world.' Earl King: the first he heard say funky about music. I'm Walkin's opening: 'the quintessential New Orleans bass drum lick, taken straight from Black New Orleans's parades.' On Little Richard: 'the only reason I started playing what they come to call a rock-and-roll beat came from trying to match Richard's right hand ... Most everything I had done before was a shuffle or slow triplets ... on Tutti Frutti, you can hear me playing a shuffle.' Scherman: Slippin' and Slidin', 7 February 1956, the first time he matched Richard's straight eighths note for note.

title: Greg Villepique, review of Backbeat: Earl Palmer's Story, Salon, 31 August 1999
notes: Quotes the book: 'I lived in a jazz world. I was not interested in Little Richard or Fats Domino ... It's something we did that was not important to us musically.' Calls him 'generally credited with inventing rock 'n' roll drumming'; Little Richard's 'pile-driving style forced Palmer to create an equally powerful backbeat'.

title: 'In Memoriam: The Great Earl Palmer', WWOZ, September 2008
notes: Born in the Seventh Ward, Tremé, 24 October 1924; died 19 September 2008 in Los Angeles, aged 83. First session in 1947 for Dave Bartholomew. The Fat Man 'and all the rest of Domino's hits', Tutti Frutti and most of Richard's early hits, Lawdy Miss Clawdy, I Hear You Knockin'. Television themes: Ironside, The Odd Couple, 77 Sunset Strip, The Brady Bunch. 'Palmer's real passion was jazz; he always considered rock and roll as his day job.'

title: Associated Press obituary, 'Earl Palmer', via Legacy.com, September 2008
notes: 'The session drummer whose pioneering backbeats were recorded on such classics as Little Richard's Tutti Frutti and The Righteous Brothers' You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin'.' Died at his Los Angeles home, aged 84. Little Richard wrote in his autobiography that Palmer 'is probably the greatest session drummer of all time'.

title: 'Earl Palmer', Drummer Cafe, featured drummers
notes: Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2000 with Hal Blaine, 'whom he mentored in the late 50s and occasionally doubled up with on recording sessions'. 'Marked by a preternatural sense of propulsion and delightfully sly fills.'

title: New Orleans Drumming: From R&B to Funk, with Earl Palmer and Herman Ernest (DCI Music Video, 1993), YouTube SZMQSPs_l1k
notes: Palmer, 68, at a red Yamaha kit with chrome hardware, a metal snare and Zildjians, with a tenor saxophonist; seen in close-up at 5:00, 7:00 and 8:00, at the kit at 18:00, from behind at 25:00, and the kit whole with a tenor player at 10:00. Short black hair grey at the temples, a grey and black moustache; a pale yellow polo neck under a grey-brown tweed jacket.

title: The Fat Man (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Fats Domino and Dave Bartholomew; recorded at J&M, New Orleans, Saturday 10 December 1949; Domino, Earl Palmer, Frank Fields, Ernest McLean, Herbert Hardesty, Clarence Hall, Joe Harris, Red Tyler. 'Earl Palmer said it was the first time a drummer played nothing but back beat for recording, which he said he derived from a Dixieland out chorus.'

title: Lawdy Miss Clawdy - Wikipedia
notes: Lloyd Price, recorded at J&M, 13 March 1952, with Bartholomew's band: Salvador Doucette (piano; Fats Domino also on the date), Ernest McLean, Frank Fields, Earl Palmer, Herbert Hardesty and Joe Harris. 'Loping, midtempo shuffle beats with their busy ride cymbal', and the snare on 2 and 4, 'which led him to be referred to as the father of the backbeat'.

title: Tutti Frutti (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded 14 September 1955 in three takes, about fifteen minutes; Lee Allen and Red Tyler, Huey Smith, Frank Fields, Justin Adams and Earl Palmer. The refrain 'a verbal rendition of a drum pattern imagined by Little Richard'.

title: Long Tall Sally - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded 7 February 1956 at J&M, released March 1956 backed with Slippin' and Slidin'. 'Richard plays staccato straight eighth notes while drummer Earl Palmer plays a fast shuffle.'

title: Ready Teddy - Wikipedia
notes: Little Richard with Lee Allen, Alvin 'Red' Tyler, Edgar Blanchard, Frank Fields and Earl Palmer. Sung by Elvis Presley on The Ed Sullivan Show, 9 September 1956.

title: Slow Down (Larry Williams song) - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded at Master Recorders, Hollywood, 11 September 1957; the Beatles' version, 1 June 1964.

title: Rockin' Robin (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Written by Leon René as Jimmie Thomas; Bobby Day, Class Records, 1958.

title: Summertime Blues - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded 28 March 1958 at Gold Star, Hollywood; Connie 'Guybo' Smith on electric bass and Earl Palmer on drums.

title: Donna (Ritchie Valens song) - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded 16 September 1958 at Gold Star, Los Angeles; Bob Keane the session leader, Earl Palmer on drums, Buddy Clark on bass, Valens, René Hall, Irving Ashby and Carol Kaye on guitars.

title: La Bamba (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Valens's 1958 rock and roll version with Buddy Clark (string bass), Ernie Freeman (piano), Carol Kaye (acoustic rhythm guitar), René Hall (Danelectro baritone guitar) and Earl Palmer (drums and claves).

title: You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' - Wikipedia
notes: Phil Spector's production for the Righteous Brothers, 1964, at Gold Star; Barney Kessel on guitar and Earl Palmer on drums among the players; Larry Levine: the guitars, pianos, basses and horns recorded first, 'then finally the drums'.
